Nodes.Text: Speak softly. Here we listen to the one whose sleep keeps our lamps. We call him the Rooted. The plume is his body; we do not pretend otherwise.

Choices.Text: How may I be trusted here?
May I sleep on the plume?
You recognized me before I spoke.

Nodes.Text: Beyond that eastern wall, through more stone than either of us can name, the First Root sleeps. He has held his arms open toward it for a thousand years. We leave the space before his fingertips untouched. Please walk around it.

Attend to a name before asking to enter a dream. Our founding-wall tender needs a chip of tepuibone to support an old inscription. The pale seams on the Stump's slopes will yield one. Bring it to her, and hear the name she is keeping. A gift does not erase harm done to the patch.

Choices.Text: I will speak with the tender.

Nodes.Text: You have a place beside our light. Stand on the living plume beside his torso, then lie down and sleep. Use the plume underfoot; the stone beside it is only stone. If danger is near, wait. When you wake, keep whatever fragments remain. He is content to hold us; that is the first thing most visitors understand.
Patch-bloom. It stays with those who have slept in his arms for a few weeks. I knew you had been spoken to. I do not know what he said; that belongs to you.
Then you have met him. You need not make the fragments into a speech for me. Some things he keeps for the Root; some he leaves with a guest. Sit beside the light as long as you need.

Keep the lamp low. This name is older than the hands that taught my hands. A chip of tepuibone will hold the weakened edge while I recut the last syllable. If you bring one from the Stump's slopes, stay and hear the name with me. That is the service; the stone is how we begin.

Choices.Text: Place one tepuibone chip beside the inscription and listen.
Tell me how you tend him.
Leave the lamp where it is.

Nodes.Text: We clean a stalk, turn a lamp, speak a name. Elsewhere they may say they tend a patch and mean him quietly. Here we address him. The light comes out of his chest. Harm it and every hearth of our people will know an enemy; this is no ordinary bed of mushrooms.
And it will outlast both our hands. The Listening elder will explain how to lie upon the founding plume. There is no second payment to make.
